title: Shortest Word Distance III
statement:
You are given a list of words `wordsDict` and two strings `word1` and `word2`, both of which appear in the list. Return the smallest gap `|i - j|` over all pairs of positions `i` and `j` with `wordsDict[i] == word1` and `wordsDict[j] == word2`.

`word1` and `word2` may be the same string. In that case the two positions must be different, so the answer is the smallest gap between two separate occurrences of that word. The input guarantees such a pair exists (a repeated word appears at least twice).
constraints: wordsDict[i] contains only lowercase English letters
word1 and word2 both appear in wordsDict
If word1 == word2, it appears at least twice
signature: int shortestWordDistance(String[] wordsDict, String word1, String word2)
notes:
## Intuition

The simple idea lists every position of `word1` and every position of `word2` and tries all pairs, which is O(n²) in the worst case. But the closest partner of a position is always the most recent one seen before it (or the next one after, which will look back at it). So one left-to-right scan that remembers the latest index of each word is enough.

When the two words are the same, a single word has to play both roles: the latest occurrence and the one before it.

## Approach

1. Note whether `word1` and `word2` are equal in `same`. Set `last1` and `last2` to -1 (not seen) and `best` to `wordsDict.length`, which is larger than any gap.
2. Walk `i` over the list.
3. If the word is `word1`: when `same`, first move the previous `last1` into `last2`; then set `last1 = i`.
4. Otherwise, if it is `word2`, set `last2 = i`.
5. Once both indices are known, update `best` with `|last1 - last2|`.
6. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`word1 = "makes"`, `word2 = "coding"`. At `i = 1` "makes" sets `last1 = 1`. At `i = 3` "coding" sets `last2 = 3`, so `best = 2`. At `i = 4` "makes" sets `last1 = 4`, and `|4 - 3| = 1` improves `best` to `1`, the answer.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · L): one pass, with word comparisons of length at most L = 10.
- Space: O(1): three indices and a flag.

## Pitfalls

- With equal words, checking `word1` and then `word2` with two separate `if`s sets both indices to the same `i` and reports a gap of 0. Use `else if` and shift the old index instead.
- Do not stop at the first pair found; a closer pair may come later.
- Initialising `best` with `Infinity` works in JavaScript, but a bound like the list length keeps it an integer in typed languages.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `same` | whether both words are the same string |
| `last1` | latest index of `word1` (-1 if none yet) |
| `last2` | latest index of `word2`, or the previous occurrence when `same` |
| `best` | smallest gap found so far |
| `i` | current position in `wordsDict` |
